job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

response.passage: In the science lab, Ms. Anjali set up an experiment to test liquid conductivity. Rohan dipped two copper wires into a beaker of distilled water, but the LED did not light up. 'Is the battery dead?' Rohan asked. Ms. Anjali shook her head, 'No, distilled water is a poor conductor. Unlike tap water, it lacks the dissolved salts that allow electricity to flow.' She then added a pinch of salt, and the LED glowed brightly. 'Now, look at the electrodes,' she pointed out. 'The copper ions from the solution are moving to the spoon to form a coating, a process called electroplating.' Priya asked, 'Does the electricity turn into metal?' Ms. Anjali smiled, 'Not at all. The metal atoms travel through the liquid to deposit on the object. Finally, notice the bubbles forming; this is not boiling, but the chemical breakdown of water into gases.' Rohan then tried to reverse the LED wires, and it stopped glowing. 'Ah,' he realized, 'the LED has a specific polarity.' Ms. Anjali nodded, 'Exactly. It only works when the long leg connects to the positive terminal.'
response.summary: The passage explains that distilled water is a poor conductor compared to salt water. It also clarifies that electroplating involves the movement of metal ions through a liquid, not the creation of metal from electricity.
